paras: The lynching of Nathan Laird was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that took him from the jail at Sardis, Mississippi, early on the morning of June 21, 1882. Laird, named 'Nathan Lucid' in the wire report and 'Frank Layard' in a Memphis paper, was awaiting trial on a charge of raping or assaulting members of a white widow's household. The Sardis paper gave a detailed account of the jail raid, while papers across the country carried a one-sentence wire item.

According to the Panola Weekly Star of Sardis, Laird was accused of entering the house of Mrs. Taylor, a widow living seven or eight miles east of town, after midnight on the night before Friday, June 16, and raping her daughter after striking Mrs. Taylor in the face with a pistol. The Memphis Public Ledger gave a different version, in which he beat the widow insensible and was driven off before he could rape her by her thirteen-year-old daughter, who scorched his face with a firebrand.

The Star reported that he was found asleep on the gallery of Gabe Wells in Sardis with his face 'marked up with smut', later arrested in a gully near town, and brought before 'Squire Balch. The paper conceded that all the evidence was circumstantial and that no trial had been held, but said he was jailed to await a trial set for Wednesday. On Tuesday, according to the Star, he told 'certain parties' he was the man sought but denied doing more than striking Mrs. Taylor and threatening her daughter.

About half past one that night, roughly seventy-five masked horsemen came to the jail and demanded the prisoner. Deputy sheriff George V. Lester and Sheriff Smith, who was sick in bed, each refused to give up the keys. When the leader ordered the doors broken down, saying they had come for the prisoner and 'were going to have him', the sheriff's wife handed over the keys, and Lester was taken upstairs to point out the cell.

Laird cried 'murder' as the cell was opened; he was rushed across the courthouse yard, put on a mule, and taken out East Lee street while guards posted at street corners rejoined the column. The Star placed the hanging at a small oak tree about a mile from town, while the Public Ledger said he was hanged to a tree limb some four miles east of Sardis between one and two o'clock. The Star's headline says the body remained hanging eight hours, though the surviving text breaks off before describing it.

The Star's headline announced a verdict of the coroner's jury, but its text is not preserved, and no report of arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage. Laird's mother and other relatives refused to bury him, saying, as the Star rendered it, that they 'wanted dem dat hung him to bury him', and he was buried at county expense.

A brief Jackson dispatch dated June 21 carried the story nationally, reporting that an armed mob took 'Nathan Lucid, colored' from the jail and hanged him. Papers varied the charge as 'rape', 'indecent assault', 'felonious assault' or 'brutal assault', and the Savannah Morning News added that 'the lynchers are unknown'. Garbled versions placed the town in Wisconsin, as in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, and the New-York Tribune had the mob entering 'the Crown Court'.

Headlines such as 'Negro Hanged by a Mob' and the Memphis Daily Appeal's 'Negro Rapist Lynched' named the victim's race, and the Bismarck Tribune called him 'a rapist' outright. Weekly crime columns in Dakota and Michigan repeated the item into late June, saying he was lynched 'for criminal assault upon a white woman'.

The two regional accounts treated the accusation as proven: the Public Ledger called him 'a darky' and 'the wretch' and said the lynchers were 'said to be strangers' from the neighborhood of the assault. The Star headlined him as a rapist and called the crime a 'fiendish deed', yet it also praised the sheriff and deputy for trying to save the prisoner.

reader.title: Lynching of Nathan Laird
bases: A mob of masked horsemen took an accused Black prisoner from the Sardis jail and hanged him (A18, A1, A2).

A company of about seventy-five masked men forced the keys from the sheriff's household, took the prisoner awaiting trial on a rape charge, and hanged him (A18, A1); every report calls it a mob hanging of a man 'charged with' rape or assault (A2, A3, A5).
The local Panola Star (A18), the Memphis Public Ledger's separate account (A1), and the Jackson wire (A2, A3, A5) agree that a mob took the man from the Sardis jail early on June 21 and hanged him.

accounts.label: Local paper (Panola Weekly Star)
accounts.gist: Laird was jailed on circumstantial evidence for raping Mrs. Taylor's daughter; about seventy-five masked horsemen forced the keys from the sheriff's household at 1:30 a.m., took him out East Lee street about a mile to an oak tree, and hanged him.

accounts.label: Memphis Public Ledger
accounts.gist: 'Frank Layard' had beaten the widow Taylor insensible and was driven off by her thirteen-year-old daughter with a firebrand; a large force of men, said to be strangers, took him from the jailer and hanged him four miles east of Sardis.

accounts.label: Jackson wire
accounts.gist: An armed mob forcibly entered the county jail early on June 21, took Nathan Lucid, colored, charged with rape or indecent assault, and hanged him; the lynchers were unknown.

framing.detail: The Sardis Star headlined the prisoner as a rapist, called the crime a 'fiendish deed' and 'hellish work' while conceding no trial was had and the evidence was circumstantial, and praised the sheriff and deputy for refusing the keys.
The Memphis Public Ledger called the victim 'a darky' and 'the wretch', treated his guilt as fact, and praised the 'gallant girl' who burned him.
Most papers ran a one-sentence Jackson wire under headings such as 'Negro Hanged by a Mob' or 'Negro Rapist Lynched', with the charge stated as an accusation.

conflicts.note: All describe one prisoner taken from the Sardis jail; the local Star's 'Laird' is the closest source.
